chunks.locator: Master project — predicting a model's final quality from a partial training run
chunks.heading: Master project — predicting a model's final quality from a partial training run
chunks.text: The question. Training large models is expensive. Teams want to stop weak runs early, but early loss curves are noisy and easy to misread. Can you forecast the final validation loss of a run from only the first fraction of its learning curve? What I built. A pipeline that forecasts final validation loss from a partial curve, using two foundation-model families for the prediction — ifBO/FT-PFN and TabPFN-style predictors — and 14 different strategies for choosing which previously completed runs to condition the prediction on. Experiments ran across four model scales, from small to large, as batch jobs on a Slurm cluster. What I found. Two things.

chunks.locator: Master project — predicting a model's final quality from a partial training run
chunks.heading: Master project — predicting a model's final quality from a partial training run
chunks.text: What I found. Two things. First, which context strategies transfer from small scales to large ones, which is the practically useful question: you want to tune the strategy cheaply on small runs and have it still work where the compute actually goes. Second, the two model families differ sharply in how stable their uncertainty is. That second finding only appears if you judge predictions by interval scores and coverage rather than by point accuracy — a model can have a good mean prediction and untrustworthy error bars at the same time. Why the evaluation mattered more than the model.

chunks.locator: Master project — predicting a model's final quality from a partial training run
chunks.heading: Master project — predicting a model's final quality from a partial training run
chunks.text: Why the evaluation mattered more than the model. A large part of the work was making the comparison fair: normalisation choices and how past runs are subsampled both move the results, so I had to separate genuine differences between the predictors from artefacts of the experimental setup. I also measured how sensitive each family is to how the observed prefix of the curve is sampled, and found one family far more sensitive than the other — which meant some earlier robustness claims did not hold up under a broader sampler. Stack. Python, PyTorch, TabPFN, pandas, NumPy, matplotlib, Slurm.

chunks.locator: AutoML lab project — searching for an architecture and its hyperparameters at once
chunks.heading: AutoML lab project — searching for an architecture and its hyperparameters at once
chunks.text: The question. Architecture and hyperparameters are usually tuned separately, so a promising architecture can be discarded just because it was tested with bad settings. What happens if you search over both together under one shared budget? What I built. A joint neural architecture search and hyperparameter optimisation pipeline over convolutional models on Fashion-MNIST, comparing search strategies against a random-search baseline under an equal budget. Result. A working end-to-end AutoML pipeline, plus a practical read on where a limited search budget actually pays off versus where it is wasted. Stack. Python, PyTorch, NAS, HPO.

chunks.locator: Switching Optimizers — a reinforcement-learning agent that picks the optimizer
chunks.heading: Switching Optimizers — a reinforcement-learning agent that picks the optimizer
chunks.text: The question. Different optimizers suit different loss-surface topologies, and practitioners debate switching mid-training (Adam early, SGD late) with little controlled evidence. Can an agent learn when to switch? What I built. With three coursemates at the University of Freiburg, we formulated the optimization process as a reinforcement-learning environment: an agent interacts with a range of objective functions and is rewarded for choosing the right algorithm at each step, so it learns a policy rather than a fixed schedule. We benchmarked on low-dimensional white-box problems first, then on unseen tasks. Result.

chunks.locator: Switching Optimizers — a reinforcement-learning agent that picks the optimizer
chunks.heading: Switching Optimizers — a reinforcement-learning agent that picks the optimizer
chunks.text: We benchmarked on low-dimensional white-box problems first, then on unseen tasks. Result. An agent that outperformed tuned standard optimizers, including on tasks it had not seen during training. We also found the soft agent's performance was extremely sensitive to the initial point, which is the kind of caveat that belongs next to the headline. Presented as a research poster. Stack. Python, PyTorch, reinforcement learning, benchmarking.

chunks.heading: LLM code-review evaluation (in progress)
chunks.text: The question. Can an LLM tell when it is wrong about code? Not "can it find bugs", but: is its confidence in a review finding calibrated enough that you could safely auto-accept its high-confidence suggestions? What I built so far. A matched-pair benchmark. For every buggy function mined from a real fix commit, the corpus also contains the fixed version of the same function — same repo, same style, one difference. That gives a false-positive rate on a matched distribution, which is what makes a detection rate meaningful. 690 pairs from 11 maintained Python repositories, with every model call cached so results can be reproduced without re-spending tokens. The honest status.

chunks.heading: LLM code-review evaluation (in progress)
chunks.text: The honest status. I audited 30 pairs by hand against the requirement that the bug be findable from the shown function alone, and only 43% passed — many mined fixes are real but only diagnosable with repo-wide context the benchmark never shows the model. I tried two filtering strategies (commit-message patterns, and structural analysis of the fix shape) and measured both as failures rather than quietly keeping the better number. The corpus is committed with that limitation recorded instead of being presented as a clean benchmark, and the planned fix is a second arm of synthetic injected bugs where locality holds by construction. Stack. Python, git and AST mining, pytest.

chunks.heading: This site's question-answering bot
chunks.text: The question. A retrieval bot is easy to build and proves little, so: can I say how good the retriever actually is, and how often the bot fabricates when asked something my documents do not cover? What I built. The widget answering this question. Retrieval runs entirely in the browser over an index built from my public documents — BM25 and a reduced TF-IDF (LSA) retriever, plus a hybrid of the two — and only the final answer is generated by a model, behind a rate-limited proxy that holds the API key. Behind it is a set of hand-labelled questions, including deliberately out-of-scope ones, so recall and the refusal rate are measured numbers rather than an impression.

chunks.heading: Conclusion
chunks.text: Conclusion ● Extrapolating small-scale curves to larger scales is feasible ● Which hyperparameters you include matters more than how many curves you use ● Predictions fit the observed region well but miss late-stage bends, even with full context - extrapolation has a ceiling ● ifBO is also sensitive to hyperparameter ordering, unlike TabPFN - a practical robustness gap ● ifBO beats Tab PFN early, but TabPFN catches up and overtakes as more of the target is observed ● Overall, ifBO offers real value for early-stage forecasting, but isn't a clear winner across the board - the right choice depends on how much of the curve you've already observed. 15

chunks.heading: Why Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) ?
chunks.text: Why Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) ? • Supervised learning requires a lot of labelled data • Getting good quality labelled data is usually expensive and time-consuming Motivation for SSL: Learning useful representations of the data by leveraging unlabelled data pool, which is easier to acquire SSL has been successfully applied in NLP field (e.g: BERT, GPT-3, etc.)

chunks.heading: Contrastive Learning
chunks.text: Contrastive Learning One direction for SSL is contrastive learning Goal of contrastive learning : To learn such an embedding space in which similar sample pairs stay close to each other while dissimilar ones are far apart Examples of contrastive learning frameworks: • SimCLR (Cheng et al, 2020) & SimCLR-v2 (2020) • MoCo (He et al, 2019) & MoCo-v2 (2020)

chunks.heading: SimCLR & MoCo (MoCo-v2)
chunks.text: SimCLR & MoCo (MoCo-v2) SimCLR and MoCo have four major components: • Data augmentation • Base Encoder f (ResNet) • Projection head g • Contrastive Loss However, MoCo is more computing- efficient due to: • Slow-moving average network (momentum • encoder) Dynamic dictionary look-up (memory bank) These methods need careful treatments of negative pairs Image source: https://generallyintelligent.ai/blog/2020-08-24-understanding-self-supervised-contrastive-learning/

chunks.heading: DINO (Self-Distillation with No Labels)
chunks.text: DINO (Self-Distillation with No Labels) DINO interprets the existing BYOL framework with a few changes: • Core architecture is Vision Transformer (can be flexible) • Self-distillation: • Two separate networks - student and teacher (same as target and online network in BYOL) • However, the final loss is cross-entropy (as proposed in Knowledge Distillation paper) • Collapse prevention by centering and sharpening of the teacher output

chunks.text: How DINO works same architecture 1. Forward Training Phase • All crops are passed through the student • Only the global views are passed through the teacher

chunks.heading: Key takeaways
chunks.text: Key takeaways • Teacher and Student network have the same architecture but different parameters • Teacher is not trained beforehand but is trained along with the student network • Multi-cropping is used to create global and local views of the image ▪Encourage “local-to-global” correspondences • Student parameters are updated via backpropagation of the loss function • Teacher parameters are updated via EMA using earlier student parameters • Sharpening and Centering in DINO has the effect of preventing mode collapse, analogous to batch normalization in BYOL

chunks.heading: Comparing with other SSL frameworks
chunks.text: Comparing with other SSL frameworks • DINO performance is second best (only behind supervised learning • Can be combined with ResNet50 and manage to achieve remarkable results • When combining DINO with ViT, k-NN classifier is almost on par with linear classifier

chunks.heading: Why is DINO so powerful?
chunks.text: Why is DINO so powerful? It turns out, applying self-supervision to Vision Transformers leads to the following desirable properties: • The model learns to semantically segment the object and create boundaries. This information is accessible in the self-attention modules • The learned feature representations i.e., the output vector of the model, is very useful to perform clustering ⮚ Allow fast classification (i.e: k-NN)

chunks.heading: Importance of the different components
chunks.text: Importance of the different components • Without Momentum, DINO failed to converge. • Predictor is required for BYOL to avoid collapse, but not for DINO • Multi-crop and cross-entropy loss are important components to obtain good features in DINO

chunks.heading: Impact of the choice of Teacher Network
chunks.text: Impact of the choice of Teacher Network Student copy and Previous iter fail to converge. Momentum encoder yields the best result, followed by Previous epoch. - Teacher always outperforms student when using momentum encoder => Help guide the student

chunks.heading: Impact of the choice of Teacher Network
chunks.text: Impact of the choice of Teacher Network Two forms of collapse: • Model output is uniform along all dimensions (high entropy) • Model output is dominated by one dimension (low entropy) • Centering avoids the collapse induced by a domin dimension, but encourages an uniform output. • Sharpening induces the opposite effect.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Summary Self-supervised learning such as DINO • Can learn SOTA self-supervised representations without requiring negatives ⮚ Surpassing even supervised learning for segmentation ⮚ Nearly surpassing supervised learning for classification • Have emerged properties that can be leveraged in future applications 1. Features quality has potential for k-NN classification and image retrieval 2. Scene layout information can also benefit weakly supervised image segmentation • Manage to achieve performance comparable with the best convnets with the same setting ⮚ Could be the key to developing a BERT-like model based on ViT

chunks.heading: SimCLR
chunks.text: SimCLR Two transformations v and v' of x are fed through the same network to produce two projections z and z’ The contrastive loss will: • Maximize the similarity of z and z’ from the same input x • Minimize the similarity to projections of other images within the same mini-batch SimCLR relies on large batch training, in order to ensure a sufficiently diverse set of negatives computationally demanding ❌ Image source: Google AI Blog: Advancing Self-Supervised and Semi-Supervised Learning with SimCLR (googleblog.com)

chunks.heading: MoCo & MoCo-v2 - Momentum Contrast
chunks.text: MoCo & MoCo-v2 - Momentum Contrast • Dynamic dictionary look-up keeps a queue of encoded feature representations from the current and previous batches. Solve the batch size problem ✓ • Slow-moving average network (momentum encoder) is adopted to improve the representation consistency between the current and earlier keys. Better results compared to SimCLR ✓ However, similar to SimCLR, MoCo also requires careful treatment of negative pairs ❌ Image source: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4VVGtYPM8JE

chunks.heading: Knowledge Distillation
chunks.text: Knowledge Distillation • A primary mechanism that enables humans to quickly learn new complex concepts when given only small training sets with the same or different categories • In deep learning, KD is an effective technique that has been widely used to transfer information from one network to another network whilst training constructively • KD was first defined and generalized by Hinton et al • KD has been broadly applied to two distinct fields: model compression and knowledge transfer

chunks.heading: Self-Distillation
chunks.text: Self-Distillation • Definition: The goal of self-distillation is to learn a student model by distilling knowledge in itself without referring to other models • Another definition: When both the student and teacher are the same network, then it is called as Self-Distillation

chunks.heading: A Generalizable Approach to Learning
chunks.text: A Generalizable Approach to Learning Optimizers Diogo Almeida Clemens Winter Jie Tang Wojciech Zaremba OpenAI Presenter: Huy Hoang Dang DAC seminar WS22/23 Albert-Ludwigs-Universität Freiburg

chunks.heading: Outline
chunks.text: Outline ▪ Motivation ▪ Introduction to LHOPT ▪ Problem setup 1. Feature space 2. Action space 3. Reward Function 4. Inner Optimizer ▪ Results ▪ Limitations ▪ Conclusion ▪ References 2

chunks.heading: Motivation
chunks.text: Motivation • Previous works of “learning to optimize” attempt to learn a general update rule from scratch. → Quite promising, even outperforming human-designed optimizers in specific tasks. • But testing these results in out-of-distribution, they have shown limited generalization. E.g: image-based datasets do not work in text-based datasets. • Therefore, the proposed method manages to generalize to different tasks without tuning. 3

chunks.heading: LHOPT – Learned Hyperparameters
chunks.text: LHOPT – Learned Hyperparameters OPTimizers ▪ A generalization-first perspective ▪ Leverages the priors of existing optimization algorithms, such as Adam. ▪ Can be interpreted as having data-driven schedules that interpolate with hand-designed optimizers. 4

chunks.heading: LHOPT – Learned Hyperparameters
chunks.text: LHOPT – Learned Hyperparameters OPTimizers ▪ Learning to update hyperparameters (e.g: learning rate, weight decay, etc.) instead of parameters. ▪ This affords two main axes of decoupling: o Network architecture o Frequency at which the policy has to run 5

chunks.heading: Problem setup
chunks.text: Problem setup ▪ Inner steps – Applying the learned optimizer to an inner optimization task (optimizee). ▪ Outer steps – Collect input statistics from the inner steps (e.g validation loss) to update hyperparameters for the inner optimizer. 6

chunks.heading: Problem setup (cont.)
chunks.text: Problem setup (cont.) ▪ Feature space ▪ Action space ▪ Reward function ▪ Inner Optimizer 7

chunks.heading: Feature Space
chunks.text: Feature Space ▪ Most of the features are unitless features (e.g: log-ratio, cosine similarity, etc.) ▪ Different from existing learned optimizers, which use only statistics such as the gradient, square of gradient, and loss values. ▪ → Prevent the policy from inferring with the inner optimization task. 8

chunks.heading: Feature Space
chunks.text: Feature Space ▪ CDF (Cumulative distribution function) feature is novel since: • There are use cases for which we would like to know the relative values of a feature within an inner task. • Ranking features should be invariant to details of the inner task. 9

chunks.heading: Action space
chunks.text: Action space ▪ Two ways of updating hyperparameters: - Scaling (multiplying by a constant) - Logit shifting → Making the model more robust by adding relative actions and randomness 10

chunks.heading: Action space (cont.)
chunks.text: Action space (cont.) ▪ Additional class of actions – learning to restart from checkpoints ▪ Three actions per checkpoint: - Save current state - Load state - Swap states - Do nothing ▪ Ideas: - Learned optimizer should be able to undertake task-specific tuning. - Can be learned with Population Based Training (PBT). - Help with exploration while training by • Decreasing the length of credit assignment paths • Less punishing to sample suboptimal settings. 11

chunks.heading: Reward function
chunks.text: Reward function ▪ Evaluate a baseline on the same problem with all task-specific values and initial weights. ▪ Take all points on the learning curve of the baseline then fits a power law curve. This results in a function where: - 0 corresponds to the worst loss - 1 to the best loss - values greater than 1 take into account how difficult that problem 12

chunks.heading: Inner Optimizer
chunks.text: Inner Optimizer Designed Customizable Inner Adaptive Optimizer (CIAO)(1) to work with LHOPT formulation • Existing optimizers have been designed to work with mostly static hyperparameters and minimal hyperparameter tuning. • Easily create new optimization techniques as well as ease of tuning. (1) https://github.com/openai/LHOPT 13

chunks.heading: Limitations
chunks.text: Limitations ▪ 1. This metric ignores how much better or worse the models are than baselines. ▪ 2. Since training loss and validation loss are also used as features, overfitting to the validation set might occur. ▪ 3. A single run cannot provide an exact measurement of a speedup; it can only provide an approximate upper or lower bound. ▪ 4. … 24

chunks.heading: Conclusion
chunks.text: Conclusion ▪ The generalization-first approach used in this study makes LHOPTs more useful and effective. - Due to high computing costs, inability to be generalized, etc., previous efforts train update rules from scratch, which is not really feasible in the real world. ▪ My opinion: - The performance and stability can be enhanced because of overfitting problems and the metric's limitations. - This approach is relatively new, so really looking forward to improvements. 25
